title: Oases of Fire in the Dark Sea

passage.title: Oases of Fire in the Dark Sea
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Two miles beneath the ocean waves, the last trace of sunlight fades into pitch blackness. Down on the sea floor, the water hovers near freezing. The weight of the sea above crushes almost everything in its path. For decades, scientists assumed this deep zone was a barren desert where food was too scarce to support large groups of animals. Without sun rays to power green plants, only a thin rain of dead scraps from the surface could feed the bottom. Yet in 1977, a sub diving near the Galapagos Islands found a rich world around tall rock chimneys.

These chimneys, known as hydrothermal vents, form along cracks where great plates of Earth's crust pull apart. Cold seawater continues to seep down through tiny fractures in the ocean floor. There it nears hot melted rock. Heated past the boiling point and loaded with dissolved minerals, the dark plumes of water are blasted upward into the icy sea by immense underground pressure. When this scalding fluid hits the frigid ocean, the minerals cool fast and harden into towers called black smokers. Some of these jagged rock spires rise as high as a ten-story building.

To a human, the water pouring from a black smoker would be a deadly poison full of sulfur gas. However, billions of tiny bacteria live inside the warm clouds. They coat the rocks like thick white mats. Because no sunlight reaches the seabed, these hardy microbes perform a process called chemosynthesis instead of using light. They capture energy from the sulfur in the vent water and use it to build sugars. In this dark realm, tiny bacteria replace green plants as the base of the food web.

Because the microbes make so much food, strange and vivid creatures thrive right beside the steaming chimneys. Giant tube worms as tall as a person anchor themselves to the rock walls. These worms have no mouth and no stomach at all. Instead, they pack their red plumes and inner tissues with billions of sulfur-eating bacteria that make food for them from the inside. Pale blind shrimp, ghost-white crabs, and pink vent fish weave between the tubes to graze on the mats.

A single vent field does not last forever on the shifting ocean floor. If an earthquake seals the rock cracks below, the hot mineral flow stops. The chimney grows cold within months. Even so, young tube worm larvae drift on deep currents until they sense the chemical trail of a new vent miles away. These hidden oases prove that life does not always need the sun to flourish on Earth.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"Heated past the boiling point and loaded with dissolved minerals, the dark plumes of water are blasted upward into the icy sea by immense underground pressure."

In this sentence, what force actually pushes the dark plumes of water upward?

options.text: The icy sea pushing down on the dissolved minerals
options.childFeedback: The icy sea is where the hot plumes end up after they are blasted upward, not the force pushing them up from below.

options.text: Immense underground pressure beneath the ocean floor
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'are blasted upward into the icy sea by immense underground pressure' identifies immense underground pressure as the force pushing the water plumes up.

options.text: The dissolved minerals floating toward the sunlight
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 explains that no sunlight reaches two miles down, and the minerals are carried inside the water plumes rather than floating toward the sun.

options.text: Propellers from the research submarine near the Galapagos Islands
options.childFeedback: The research submarine only discovered the vents in Paragraph 1; underground pressure beneath the ocean floor is what blasts the water upward in Paragraph 2.

questions.provingSentenceText: Heated past the boiling point and loaded with dissolved minerals, the dark plumes of water are blasted upward into the icy sea by immense underground pressure.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'are blasted upward into the icy sea by immense underground pressure' identifies immense underground pressure as the force pushing the water plumes up.
questions.parentExplanation: This sentence begins with two participial phrases ('Heated past...' and 'loaded with...') followed by a passive verb ('are blasted upward'). The true grammatical agent performing the action appears after the preposition 'by': 'immense underground pressure' (Option B).
questions.retryHint: Look at the end of the sentence in Paragraph 2 after 'blasted upward... by' to see what force pushes the dark plumes of water.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 1:

"For decades, scientists assumed this deep zone was a barren desert where food was too scarce to support large groups of animals."

What does the word "scarce" mean as it is used in this sentence?

options.text: Hard to find and in very short supply
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 1, 'scarce' means hard to find and in very short supply, shown by the comparison to a 'barren desert' fed only by a 'thin rain of dead scraps.'

options.text: Frightening to the animals swimming nearby
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 is explaining why scientists thought there wasn't enough food for large groups of animals, not that the food was scary.

options.text: Heated to a dangerous temperature by melted rock
options.childFeedback: The water on the normal sea floor in Paragraph 1 'hovers near freezing'; the hot melted rock isn't introduced until Paragraph 2.

options.text: Completely impossible for any living cell to digest
options.childFeedback: Even in the deep zone of Paragraph 1, a thin rain of dead scraps from the surface could still be eaten, so food was in short supply rather than impossible to digest.

questions.provingSentenceText: For decades, scientists assumed this deep zone was a barren desert where food was too scarce to support large groups of animals.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 1, 'scarce' means hard to find and in very short supply, shown by the comparison to a 'barren desert' fed only by a 'thin rain of dead scraps.'
questions.parentExplanation: The context clues 'barren desert' and 'only a thin rain of dead scraps' in Paragraph 1 confirm that 'scarce' means in very short supply (Option A). Option B confuses 'scarce' with 'scary'.
questions.retryHint: Look at the clues 'barren desert' and 'only a thin rain of dead scraps' in Paragraph 1 to see how much food scientists thought was down there.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 4, how are giant tube worms able to survive near hydrothermal vents without a mouth or a stomach?

options.text: They swim up to the ocean surface each night to feed on green plants.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 states that giant tube worms 'anchor themselves to the rock walls' two miles deep, so they never swim up to the surface.

options.text: They absorb warm sunlight through their red plumes and turn it into sugar.
options.childFeedback: Paragraphs 1 and 3 explain that zero sunlight reaches the seabed two miles down; the bacteria inside the worms use sulfur chemicals, not sunlight.

options.text: They use their sharp outer tubes to trap blind shrimp and ghost-white crabs.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 says blind shrimp and crabs weave between the tubes to graze on bacterial mats, not that the mouthless tube worms trap and eat them.

options.text: They rely on billions of bacteria living inside their bodies to turn sulfur chemicals into food.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 explains that even though giant tube worms have no mouth or stomach, billions of sulfur-eating bacteria packed inside their tissues make food for them from the inside.

questions.provingSentenceText: Instead, they pack their red plumes and inner tissues with billions of sulfur-eating bacteria that make food for them from the inside.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 4 explains that even though giant tube worms have no mouth or stomach, billions of sulfur-eating bacteria packed inside their tissues make food for them from the inside.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 4 explicitly explains the symbiotic relationship: because tube worms lack a mouth and stomach, 'they pack their red plumes and inner tissues with billions of sulfur-eating bacteria that make food for them from the inside' (Option D).
questions.retryHint: Read the third and fourth sentences of Paragraph 4 right after it mentions that the worms have no mouth and no stomach.

questions.prompt: How is the information in Paragraph 2 mainly organized?

options.text: By tracing the step-by-step cause-and-effect process that creates black smoker chimneys on the seabed
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 traces the step-by-step cause-and-effect chain: cold seawater seeps down cracks, gets heated by melted rock, blasts upward under pressure, and cools into tall black smoker towers.

options.text: By comparing the size of the Galapagos Islands to the size of a ten-story building
options.childFeedback: The last sentence of Paragraph 2 only compares the height of the rock spires to a ten-story building, not the size of the Galapagos Islands.

options.text: By listing ways that human divers can stop underground pressure from cracking the ocean floor
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 never mentions human divers trying to stop underground pressure; it explains how natural cracks and heat create hydrothermal vents.

options.text: By arguing that cold seawater is more dangerous to submarines than boiling mineral plumes
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 does not argue about submarine dangers; it explains how cold seawater gets superheated underground and builds mineral chimneys.

questions.provingSentenceText: When this scalding fluid hits the frigid ocean, the minerals cool fast and harden into towers called black smokers.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 2 traces the step-by-step cause-and-effect chain: cold seawater seeps down cracks, gets heated by melted rock, blasts upward under pressure, and cools into tall black smoker towers.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 2 uses a sequential cause-and-effect structure: seawater seeps into crust fractures, gets superheated and loaded with minerals, blasts upward into cold water, and cools into mineral towers called black smokers (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Follow the sequence of events in Paragraph 2 from cold seawater seeping down cracks to hot minerals hardening into rock towers.

questions.prompt: PART A: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?

options.text: Research submarines discovered the Galapagos Islands in 1977 while searching for sunken ships on the seabed.
options.childFeedback: The Galapagos Islands were already known long before 1977; the submarine in Paragraph 1 discovered deep-sea hydrothermal vents on the ocean floor nearby.

options.text: Black smoker chimneys often collapse after a few months when earthquakes seal the cracks in the ocean floor.
options.childFeedback: How a vent field can cool down after an earthquake is just one detail in Paragraph 5, not the main point of the entire article.

options.text: Every animal in the deep ocean must grow red plumes and lose its stomach in order to survive the freezing water.
options.childFeedback: Only the giant tube worms have red plumes and no stomachs; Paragraph 4 also mentions shrimp, crabs, and vent fish that graze on the rocks with mouths.

options.text: Deep-sea hydrothermal vents support thriving communities of life in total darkness because bacteria turn mineral chemicals into food.
options.childFeedback: Across the whole passage, the central idea is that hydrothermal vents support rich ecosystems in pitch-black water because bacteria use chemosynthesis to turn sulfur minerals into food.

questions.provingSentenceText: Because no sunlight reaches the seabed, these hardy microbes perform a process called chemosynthesis instead of using light.
questions.childTip: Across the whole passage, the central idea is that hydrothermal vents support rich ecosystems in pitch-black water because bacteria use chemosynthesis to turn sulfur minerals into food.
questions.parentExplanation: Aligned to ELAGSE5RI2, the overarching central idea spanning Paragraphs 1–5 is that hydrothermal vents sustain rich ecosystems without sunlight because chemosynthetic bacteria convert sulfur chemicals into food at the base of the food web (Option D). Option B is a Tiny Detail Trap from Paragraph 5.
questions.retryHint: Think about what surprised scientists in 1977 and how Paragraph 3 explains the way life thrives around vents without sunlight.

questions.prompt: PART B: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "Two miles beneath the ocean waves, the last trace of sunlight fades into pitch blackness."
options.childFeedback: This opening line from Paragraph 1 only describes how dark the deep ocean is, without explaining how vent bacteria support thriving life there.

options.text: "Some of these jagged rock spires rise as high as a ten-story building."
options.childFeedback: This detail from Paragraph 2 tells how tall the rock chimneys can grow, rather than proving how bacteria turn chemicals into food for the community.

options.text: "Because no sunlight reaches the seabed, these hardy microbes perform a process called chemosynthesis instead of using light."
options.childFeedback: This quotation from Paragraph 3 directly supports Question 5 by explaining how hardy microbes use chemosynthesis instead of sunlight to power the deep-sea food web.

options.text: "A single vent field does not last forever on the shifting ocean floor."
options.childFeedback: This sentence from Paragraph 5 only notes that individual vents eventually stop flowing, not how vents support life in total darkness.

questions.provingSentenceText: Because no sunlight reaches the seabed, these hardy microbes perform a process called chemosynthesis instead of using light.
questions.childTip: This quotation from Paragraph 3 directly supports Question 5 by explaining how hardy microbes use chemosynthesis instead of sunlight to power the deep-sea food web.
questions.parentExplanation: Option C directly proves the central claim in Part A by explaining the mechanism—chemosynthesis by hardy microbes in the absence of sunlight—that powers the entire hydrothermal vent ecosystem.
questions.retryHint: Find the quote from Paragraph 3 that explains how microbes make energy on the dark seabed without any sunlight.
